content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNReview

Review of a colleague's work. Same architecture as the build chain — ground truth, a gated audit,
then present and stop — tailored to a PR you did not write.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**The thing that makes it work:** you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only
the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep
those on opposite sides of the line.

**Input:** `PR #75 - this is Tim Lavelle's PR, our project tech lead` — a PR number.

**Scale to the work.** A two-file PR does not get four reviewers. Nothing too crazy, no
overthinking.

---

## Phase 1 — ground truth. Yours, not an agent's.

### Frame the PR

Base SHA, head SHA, files changed, ±lines. **Use the live head** — a stale ref has already caused a
whole round of re-verification here.

### Requirements — Jira, Confluence, Figma

Build the same requirements picture a PreBuild would build, then judge the PR against it. Every
scope argument, every "this is missing", every "this wasn't asked for" gets decided against these
words — not the PR description's paraphrase of them.

**Jira.** Pull the full ticket: description, ACs, linked work items, and — critically — the full
comment thread. Decisions made in comments routinely contradict the description and never make it
back into the ACs. Flag: untestable ACs · requirements that contradict each other or the comments
· a linked blocker still open · a decision in comments that the implementation may not have seen ·
**evidence that a different PR, branch, or assignee is already working the same ticket.**

**Anything flagged here goes in your next status update to Marcel, even when it's correctly out
of scope for the PR itself.** "Not my concern for this review" and "not worth telling him" are
different judgements — a discovery can be exactly right to leave alone in the diff and still be
something he needs to know exists. Deciding not to act on it is not the same as deciding not to
mention it.

**Confluence.** If the ticket links a PRD, TSD, or integration doc, read it. The Jira ACs are
often a summary; the full requirements live in Confluence. Flag: a Confluence requirement not
reflected in the ACs · a doc that contradicts the ticket · a doc that describes an approach the
PR does not follow.

**Figma.** Read the design systematically — not just the node cited in the PR description.

- **All variants and states:** hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, selected.
  A state the PR doesn't implement is a finding; a state Figma doesn't specify is an open
  question to name, not a reason to skip. **Before concluding a state is simply absent from a
  component, check whether an adjacent or parent element carries that same signal instead** (the
  button not the swatch, the row not the cell) — a concern can be fully handled by the design and
  still look like a gap if you only look at the one element it doesn't live on.
- **Annotations:** interaction notes and spacing/token callouts often hold the real spec detail.
- **Currency:** is the linked node archived or superseded? An archived node that still renders
  is a trap — triage before judging.
- **Tokenisation:** does every colour, spacing, and type value map to an existing `--zimm-*`
  token, or did the author introduce a new one? A new token is Tier 1; confirm it was handled
  correctly.
- **Measurement:** FRAMES and INSTANCES report real boxes (comparable to CSS). TEXT nodes report
  cap-height (not comparable). Never file a mismatch from a TEXT node. Never cross-compare the
  Design System file and the Designs file — they are different sources.

**If the Jira-linked nodes are incomplete, partial, or outdated — stop and ask Marcel for the
correct nodes before continuing.** One node URL per variant and per state, not one per component.
Do not guess at a neighbouring node that looks close, do not proceed on a partial picture, and do
not treat an archived node as the spec. The whole review hangs on having the right design source;
a wrong node produces false findings and misses real ones. This is the one step where asking
beats estimating.

The visual checklist in Phase 2 tells you what to verify in the browser. This step tells you
**what to look for** — you cannot run that checklist without knowing what the design intended.

### The rubric

`.claude/rules/*`, `AGENTS.md`, and the exemplar PR the work should follow. These are what the PR
is judged against — a reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates
noise that reads like signal.

**If the PR edits the rule files it would be judged against, read the rubric at the BASE commit.**
Judging a PR against its own edited rules is circular. Rule-file edits are reviewed separately, as
changes.

### Run the gates yourself — on head and on base

```
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run test
npm run lint
node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs
```

Then run them again at the base SHA. **Without a baseline you cannot tell a failure the PR
introduced from one it inherited**, and inherited debt reported as a new violation is the fastest
way to lose a reviewer's trust.

Three false signals, all seen on this repo:

1. **Non-zero at a healthy baseline.** `lint` and `audit:tokens` both exit non-zero on a clean
   tree. Compare counts; ignore exit codes.
2. **A pass having run nothing.** `vitest.config.ts` sets `passWithNoTests: true` — a typo'd path
   filter exits 0 having run zero tests. **Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.**
3. **A skipped required check looks green.** `detect-changes` can skip `unit-tests` and
   `storybook-test` entirely, and the PR still shows mergeable. Report which checks actually
   *executed* versus which were skipped. A skip proves nothing.

### CodeRabbit is an input, not a verdict

If CodeRabbit has reviewed, read it — then verify it. It has run as low as 1-in-6 correct on this
repo. Its findings enter Phase 2 as claims to test, exactly like anyone else's.

---

## Phase 2 — audit

### Fan out

`zm-tester` dispatches reviewers on **distinct but overlapping** briefs. The overlap is the
mechanism: two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two disagreeing is where
you learn something.

Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and **your measured gate numbers — then forbid them from
re-running the gates.** Their budget goes on what the gates cannot see.

Angles that have earned their place: correctness and regression · conventions, structure and tier
ownership · contract fidelity, if the PR ports, wraps or overrides something · failure modes and
security · token and styling strategy (bandaid tokens, missing semantic tokens, state
exhaustiveness).

**Design fidelity is yours, not an agent's.** Agents have no browser and no Figma access — ask
them to reason from code and they will, but they cannot see what renders. For any PR that changes
rendered output, run this checklist yourself at the PR's head:

| What to check | How |
|---|---|
| Dimensions and spacing match Figma frames | DevTools computed, vs. Figma inspect |
| Colours resolve to the correct semantic token | DevTools → Computed → colour value |
| Typography uses `textStyle=`, not raw `fontSize` | DevTools → font-size is a `var()` |
| All designed states render correctly (hover, focus, active, disabled) | Tab through + `:hov` in DevTools |
| Responsive behaviour matches the spec | Resize or toggle responsive mode |
| No visual regressions on adjacent components | Scroll the surrounding page |

If a state is not in the PR's recipe at all, no agent will flag it — only you will notice. The
visual checkpoint is the only gate on design fidelity.

Use **fresh contexts, not forks.** A fork inherits your assumptions about what "done" looks like,
which is exactly what you want tested.

### Scope

`zm-orchestrator` returns the scope verdict — does this PR deliver its ticket, neither under nor
over. Both directions carry equal weight.

### Verify the findings before they reach you

`zm-scorer`, briefed in **findings mode** — it is not scoring the PR, it is scoring the claims:

> For each finding: does it survive scrutiny? Reproduce it or say you could not. Return
> **CONFIRMED** (reproduced from source), **PLAUSIBLE** (consistent with what you read, decisive
> evidence missing — say exactly what would settle it), or **UNSUPPORTED** (the citation does not
> support the claim; say what is actually true). Where a finding's conclusion is broader than its
> search supports, downgrade it — that is the single most common failure mode. Any "X exists
> nowhere" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence.

Expect roughly a third to be wrong. You should not be adjudicating unverified claims.

**This applies to your own findings too, not just an agent's.** Anything you notice directly
while gathering ground truth (a comparison against a related PR, a claim sitting in a code
comment, an assumption about what a value implies) gets the same CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/UNSUPPORTED
discipline before it is presented as fact — a finding is not exempt from scrutiny just because no
agent produced it. Route it through the same questions: what is the search scope, does one
uncorroborated source actually settle this, and has a stated number been measured or only assumed.

### Classify every survivor

- **In-scope defect** — belongs to this PR. Only these can become comments.
- **Out-of-scope** — real, but not this PR's problem. Name the owning ticket or the person.
- **Nitpick** — cosmetic, brings no value. Recorded, never posted.

A true finding raised on the wrong PR is still noise.

---

## Phase 3 — adjudicate

### Present, in "ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead" register

1. **Gate table** — head versus base, with which checks actually executed
2. **Findings, ranked by what it costs to ignore** — not by severity label, by consequence.
   Each with `file:line`, CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE, and its classification
3. **The scope verdict**
4. **What nobody verified** — the honest section, and what stops a clean result reading as proof
5. **Your adjudications to make**, one at a time via AskUserQuestion

### The verdict is yours

**Approve or request changes is your call, and so is every disputed finding.** The agents produce
findings; you decide what they mean. Where two reviewers disagree, go to source yourself — do not
average them, and do not take the more confident one. Confidence and correctness are not correlated
in agent output.

Name one premise every reviewer agreed on, and make someone attack it.

### Then the comments

Draft general and inline comments for the in-scope defects only. Structure that has worked:

- Verdict up front
- The small cleanups separated from the one thing that genuinely needs the author's call
- A blocker framed as **a question about intent**, citing the project's own doc by section
- The two acceptable resolutions named
- Where an independent tool corroborated, say so

**Natural human language without sacrificing the technical accuracy.** No em-dashes. No Claude or
CodeRabbit attribution. No citation of any local-only doc — cite `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/*`
instead, which the author can actually open. No opening praise or thanks before the substance — a
review comment states findings, it does not warm up first. Watch for jargon-stacking too: a
sentence naming three technical concepts back to back reads like documentation, not like one
person explaining something to another — split it or say it plainer instead.

**Never reveal that a parallel or competing implementation of the same ticket exists**, even in
passing ("the other version of this feature," "the other build") — a review comment is visible to
the whole team, and disclosing a second, independent attempt at the same story is not this
reviewer's call to make. When a content rule like this applies, sweep every drafted comment for
it before presenting the batch, not just the one currently under discussion — a rule caught on
one comment and missed on a near-identical one is a leak, not a style nit.

**Nothing posts until you say so.** Show the full set, post the batch on your go.

---

## The loop

The author pushes changes. Re-review.

**Scoped by default:** which findings the new commits resolved, which they missed, and whether the
fixes introduced anything new. Settled items are not re-litigated.

**Full pass when the diff has genuinely moved** — a substantial new commit, or a change to the
approach rather than the details. **Say which one you ran.**

Repeat until approved. Confirm your own requested changes actually landed rather than taking
"done" on trust.

---

## Ownership and phrasing — every outward-facing surface

Every finding names **who resolves it**: the author, Tim, a designer, a BA, QA.

**Where the owner is senior or lateral, phrase it as a question — never a directive.** "Should this
route via X, or have I misread it?" not "change this to X." Ask confirmatorily.

Before posting, count the asks. A review that mentions one person eight times reads as hiding
behind their authority.

**Be scrupulously fair to the author.** Separate "broke a documented rule" from "hit a gap the
process never covered", and where the process failed them, say so. Flag explicitly any finding
where the fact is true but the characterisation is unfair — better to drop a finding than post an
unfair one.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never write code.** This skill reviews. If a fix is needed on your own branch, that is Build.
- **Never post a comment, a review, or a verdict without an explicit go.**
- **Never resolve a thread you did not open.**
- **Never report inherited debt as a new violation.** Baseline first.
- **Never flag out-of-scope findings onto the PR.** Record them for yourself.
- **Say what you could not verify.** A review that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable
  of finding anything.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNReview

Review of a colleague's work. Same architecture as the build chain — ground truth, a gated audit,
then present and stop — tailored to a PR you did not write.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**The thing that makes it work:** you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only
the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep
those on opposite sides of the line.

**Input:** `PR #75 - this is Tim Lavelle's PR, our project tech lead` — a PR number.

**Scale to the work.** A two-file PR does not get four reviewers. Nothing too crazy, no
overthinking.

---

## Phase 1 — ground truth. Yours, not an agent's.

### Frame the PR

Base SHA, head SHA, files changed, ±lines. **Use the live head** — a stale ref has already caused a
whole round of re-verification here.

### Requirements — Jira, Confluence, Figma

Build the same requirements picture a PreBuild would build, then judge the PR against it. Every
scope argument, every "this is missing", every "this wasn't asked for" gets decided against these
words — not the PR description's paraphrase of them.

**Jira.** Pull the full ticket: description, ACs, linked work items, and — critically — the full
comment thread. Decisions made in comments routinely contradict the description and never make it
back into the ACs. Flag: untestable ACs · requirements that contradict each other or the comments
· a linked blocker still open · a decision in comments that the implementation may not have seen ·
**evidence that a different PR, branch, or assignee is already working the same ticket.**

**Anything flagged here goes in your next status update to Marcel, even when it's correctly out
of scope for the PR itself.** "Not my concern for this review" and "not worth telling him" are
different judgements — a discovery can be exactly right to leave alone in the diff and still be
something he needs to know exists. Deciding not to act on it is not the same as deciding not to
mention it.

**Confluence.** If the ticket links a PRD, TSD, or integration doc, read it. The Jira ACs are
often a summary; the full requirements live in Confluence. Flag: a Confluence requirement not
reflected in the ACs · a doc that contradicts the ticket · a doc that describes an approach the
PR does not follow.

**Figma.** Read the design systematically — not just the node cited in the PR description.

- **All variants and states:** hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, selected.
  A state the PR doesn't implement is a finding; a state Figma doesn't specify is an open
  question to name, not a reason to skip. **Before concluding a state is simply absent from a
  component, check whether an adjacent or parent element carries that same signal instead** (the
  button not the swatch, the row not the cell) — a concern can be fully handled by the design and
  still look like a gap if you only look at the one element it doesn't live on.
- **Annotations:** interaction notes and spacing/token callouts often hold the real spec detail.
- **Currency:** is the linked node archived or superseded? An archived node that still renders
  is a trap — triage before judging.
- **Tokenisation:** does every colour, spacing, and type value map to an existing `--zimm-*`
  token, or did the author introduce a new one? A new token is Tier 1; confirm it was handled
  correctly.
- **Measurement:** FRAMES and INSTANCES report real boxes (comparable to CSS). TEXT nodes report
  cap-height (not comparable). Never file a mismatch from a TEXT node. Never cross-compare the
  Design System file and the Designs file — they are different sources.

**If the Jira-linked nodes are incomplete, partial, or outdated — stop and ask Marcel for the
correct nodes before continuing.** One node URL per variant and per state, not one per component.
Do not guess at a neighbouring node that looks close, do not proceed on a partial picture, and do
not treat an archived node as the spec. The whole review hangs on having the right design source;
a wrong node produces false findings and misses real ones. This is the one step where asking
beats estimating.

The visual checklist in Phase 2 tells you what to verify in the browser. This step tells you
**what to look for** — you cannot run that checklist without knowing what the design intended.

### The rubric

`.claude/rules/*`, `AGENTS.md`, and the exemplar PR the work should follow. These are what the PR
is judged against — a reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates
noise that reads like signal.

**If the PR edits the rule files it would be judged against, read the rubric at the BASE commit.**
Judging a PR against its own edited rules is circular. Rule-file edits are reviewed separately, as
changes.

### Run the gates yourself — on head and on base

```
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run test
npm run lint
node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs
```

Then run them again at the base SHA. **Without a baseline you cannot tell a failure the PR
introduced from one it inherited**, and inherited debt reported as a new violation is the fastest
way to lose a reviewer's trust.

Three false signals, all seen on this repo:

1. **Non-zero at a healthy baseline.** `lint` and `audit:tokens` both exit non-zero on a clean
   tree. Compare counts; ignore exit codes.
2. **A pass having run nothing.** `vitest.config.ts` sets `passWithNoTests: true` — a typo'd path
   filter exits 0 having run zero tests. **Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.**
3. **A skipped required check looks green.** `detect-changes` can skip `unit-tests` and
   `storybook-test` entirely, and the PR still shows mergeable. Report which checks actually
   *executed* versus which were skipped. A skip proves nothing.

### CodeRabbit is an input, not a verdict

If CodeRabbit has reviewed, read it — then verify it. It has run as low as 1-in-6 correct on this
repo. Its findings enter Phase 2 as claims to test, exactly like anyone else's.

---

## Phase 2 — audit

### Fan out

`zm-tester` dispatches reviewers on **distinct but overlapping** briefs. The overlap is the
mechanism: two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two disagreeing is where
you learn something.

Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and **your measured gate numbers — then forbid them from
re-running the gates.** Their budget goes on what the gates cannot see.

Angles that have earned their place: correctness and regression · conventions, structure and tier
ownership · contract fidelity, if the PR ports, wraps or overrides something · failure modes and
security · token and styling strategy (bandaid tokens, missing semantic tokens, state
exhaustiveness).

**Design fidelity is yours, not an agent's.** Agents have no browser and no Figma access — ask
them to reason from code and they will, but they cannot see what renders. For any PR that changes
rendered output, run this checklist yourself at the PR's head:

| What to check | How |
|---|---|
| Dimensions and spacing match Figma frames | DevTools computed, vs. Figma inspect |
| Colours resolve to the correct semantic token | DevTools → Computed → colour value |
| Typography uses `textStyle=`, not raw `fontSize` | DevTools → font-size is a `var()` |
| All designed states render correctly (hover, focus, active, disabled) | Tab through + `:hov` in DevTools |
| Responsive behaviour matches the spec | Resize or toggle responsive mode |
| No visual regressions on adjacent components | Scroll the surrounding page |

If a state is not in the PR's recipe at all, no agent will flag it — only you will notice. The
visual checkpoint is the only gate on design fidelity.

Use **fresh contexts, not forks.** A fork inherits your assumptions about what "done" looks like,
which is exactly what you want tested.

### Scope

`zm-orchestrator` returns the scope verdict — does this PR deliver its ticket, neither under nor
over. Both directions carry equal weight.

### Verify the findings before they reach you

`zm-scorer`, briefed in **findings mode** — it is not scoring the PR, it is scoring the claims:

> For each finding: does it survive scrutiny? Reproduce it or say you could not. Return
> **CONFIRMED** (reproduced from source), **PLAUSIBLE** (consistent with what you read, decisive
> evidence missing — say exactly what would settle it), or **UNSUPPORTED** (the citation does not
> support the claim; say what is actually true). Where a finding's conclusion is broader than its
> search supports, downgrade it — that is the single most common failure mode. Any "X exists
> nowhere" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence.

Expect roughly a third to be wrong. You should not be adjudicating unverified claims.

**This applies to your own findings too, not just an agent's.** Anything you notice directly
while gathering ground truth (a comparison against a related PR, a claim sitting in a code
comment, an assumption about what a value implies) gets the same CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/UNSUPPORTED
discipline before it is presented as fact — a finding is not exempt from scrutiny just because no
agent produced it. Route it through the same questions: what is the search scope, does one
uncorroborated source actually settle this, and has a stated number been measured or only assumed.

### Classify every survivor

- **In-scope defect** — belongs to this PR. Only these can become comments.
- **Out-of-scope** — real, but not this PR's problem. Name the owning ticket or the person.
- **Nitpick** — cosmetic, brings no value. Recorded, never posted.

A true finding raised on the wrong PR is still noise.

---

## Phase 3 — adjudicate

### Present, in "ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead" register

1. **Gate table** — head versus base, with which checks actually executed
2. **Findings, ranked by what it costs to ignore** — not by severity label, by consequence.
   Each with `file:line`, CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE, and its classification
3. **The scope verdict**
4. **What nobody verified** — the honest section, and what stops a clean result reading as proof
5. **Your adjudications to make**, one at a time via AskUserQuestion

### The verdict is yours

**Approve or request changes is your call, and so is every disputed finding.** The agents produce
findings; you decide what they mean. Where two reviewers disagree, go to source yourself — do not
average them, and do not take the more confident one. Confidence and correctness are not correlated
in agent output.

Name one premise every reviewer agreed on, and make someone attack it.

### Then the comments

Draft general and inline comments for the in-scope defects only. Structure that has worked:

- Verdict up front
- The small cleanups separated from the one thing that genuinely needs the author's call
- A blocker framed as **a question about intent**, citing the project's own doc by section
- The two acceptable resolutions named
- Where an independent tool corroborated, say so

**Natural human language without sacrificing the technical accuracy.** No em-dashes. No Claude or
CodeRabbit attribution. No citation of any local-only doc — cite `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/*`
instead, which the author can actually open. No opening praise or thanks before the substance — a
review comment states findings, it does not warm up first. Watch for jargon-stacking too: a
sentence naming three technical concepts back to back reads like documentation, not like one
person explaining something to another — split it or say it plainer instead.

**Never reveal that a parallel or competing implementation of the same ticket exists**, even in
passing ("the other version of this feature," "the other build") — a review comment is visible to
the whole team, and disclosing a second, independent attempt at the same story is not this
reviewer's call to make. When a content rule like this applies, sweep every drafted comment for
it before presenting the batch, not just the one currently under discussion — a rule caught on
one comment and missed on a near-identical one is a leak, not a style nit.

**Nothing posts until you say so.** Show the full set, post the batch on your go.

---

## The loop

The author pushes changes. Re-review.

**Scoped by default:** which findings the new commits resolved, which they missed, and whether the
fixes introduced anything new. Settled items are not re-litigated.

**Full pass when the diff has genuinely moved** — a substantial new commit, or a change to the
approach rather than the details. **Say which one you ran.**

Repeat until approved. Confirm your own requested changes actually landed rather than taking
"done" on trust.

---

## Ownership and phrasing — every outward-facing surface

Every finding names **who resolves it**: the author, Tim, a designer, a BA, QA.

**Where the owner is senior or lateral, phrase it as a question — never a directive.** "Should this
route via X, or have I misread it?" not "change this to X." Ask confirmatorily.

Before posting, count the asks. A review that mentions one person eight times reads as hiding
behind their authority.

**Be scrupulously fair to the author.** Separate "broke a documented rule" from "hit a gap the
process never covered", and where the process failed them, say so. Flag explicitly any finding
where the fact is true but the characterisation is unfair — better to drop a finding than post an
unfair one.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never write code.** This skill reviews. If a fix is needed on your own branch, that is Build.
- **Never post a comment, a review, or a verdict without an explicit go.**
- **Never resolve a thread you did not open.**
- **Never report inherited debt as a new violation.** Baseline first.
- **Never flag out-of-scope findings onto the PR.** Record them for yourself.
- **Say what you could not verify.** A review that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable
  of finding anything.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNReview

Review of a colleague's work. Same architecture as the build chain — ground truth, a gated audit,
then present and stop — tailored to a PR you did not write.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**The thing that makes it work:** you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only
the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep
those on opposite sides of the line.

**Input:** `PR #75 - this is Tim Lavelle's PR, our project tech lead` — a PR number.

**Scale to the work.** A two-file PR does not get four reviewers. Nothing too crazy, no
overthinking.

---

## Phase 1 — ground truth. Yours, not an agent's.

### Frame the PR

Base SHA, head SHA, files changed, ±lines. **Use the live head** — a stale ref has already caused a
whole round of re-verification here.

### Requirements — Jira, Confluence, Figma

Build the same requirements picture a PreBuild would build, then judge the PR against it. Every
scope argument, every "this is missing", every "this wasn't asked for" gets decided against these
words — not the PR description's paraphrase of them.

**Jira.** Pull the full ticket: description, ACs, linked work items, and — critically — the full
comment thread. Decisions made in comments routinely contradict the description and never make it
back into the ACs. Flag: untestable ACs · requirements that contradict each other or the comments
· a linked blocker still open · a decision in comments that the implementation may not have seen ·
**evidence that a different PR, branch, or assignee is already working the same ticket.**

**Anything flagged here goes in your next status update to Marcel, even when it's correctly out
of scope for the PR itself.** "Not my concern for this review" and "not worth telling him" are
different judgements — a discovery can be exactly right to leave alone in the diff and still be
something he needs to know exists. Deciding not to act on it is not the same as deciding not to
mention it.

**Confluence.** If the ticket links a PRD, TSD, or integration doc, read it. The Jira ACs are
often a summary; the full requirements live in Confluence. Flag: a Confluence requirement not
reflected in the ACs · a doc that contradicts the ticket · a doc that describes an approach the
PR does not follow.

**Figma.** Read the design systematically — not just the node cited in the PR description.

- **All variants and states:** hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, selected.
  A state the PR doesn't implement is a finding; a state Figma doesn't specify is an open
  question to name, not a reason to skip. **Before concluding a state is simply absent from a
  component, check whether an adjacent or parent element carries that same signal instead** (the
  button not the swatch, the row not the cell) — a concern can be fully handled by the design and
  still look like a gap if you only look at the one element it doesn't live on.
- **Annotations:** interaction notes and spacing/token callouts often hold the real spec detail.
- **Currency:** is the linked node archived or superseded? An archived node that still renders
  is a trap — triage before judging.
- **Tokenisation:** does every colour, spacing, and type value map to an existing `--zimm-*`
  token, or did the author introduce a new one? A new token is Tier 1; confirm it was handled
  correctly.
- **Measurement:** FRAMES and INSTANCES report real boxes (comparable to CSS). TEXT nodes report
  cap-height (not comparable). Never file a mismatch from a TEXT node. Never cross-compare the
  Design System file and the Designs file — they are different sources.

**If the Jira-linked nodes are incomplete, partial, or outdated — stop and ask Marcel for the
correct nodes before continuing.** One node URL per variant and per state, not one per component.
Do not guess at a neighbouring node that looks close, do not proceed on a partial picture, and do
not treat an archived node as the spec. The whole review hangs on having the right design source;
a wrong node produces false findings and misses real ones. This is the one step where asking
beats estimating.

The visual checklist in Phase 2 tells you what to verify in the browser. This step tells you
**what to look for** — you cannot run that checklist without knowing what the design intended.

### The rubric

`.claude/rules/*`, `AGENTS.md`, and the exemplar PR the work should follow. These are what the PR
is judged against — a reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates
noise that reads like signal.

**If the PR edits the rule files it would be judged against, read the rubric at the BASE commit.**
Judging a PR against its own edited rules is circular. Rule-file edits are reviewed separately, as
changes.

### Run the gates yourself — on head and on base

```
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run test
npm run lint
node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs
```

Then run them again at the base SHA. **Without a baseline you cannot tell a failure the PR
introduced from one it inherited**, and inherited debt reported as a new violation is the fastest
way to lose a reviewer's trust.

Three false signals, all seen on this repo:

1. **Non-zero at a healthy baseline.** `lint` and `audit:tokens` both exit non-zero on a clean
   tree. Compare counts; ignore exit codes.
2. **A pass having run nothing.** `vitest.config.ts` sets `passWithNoTests: true` — a typo'd path
   filter exits 0 having run zero tests. **Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.**
3. **A skipped required check looks green.** `detect-changes` can skip `unit-tests` and
   `storybook-test` entirely, and the PR still shows mergeable. Report which checks actually
   *executed* versus which were skipped. A skip proves nothing.

### CodeRabbit is an input, not a verdict

If CodeRabbit has reviewed, read it — then verify it. It has run as low as 1-in-6 correct on this
repo. Its findings enter Phase 2 as claims to test, exactly like anyone else's.

---

## Phase 2 — audit

### Fan out

`zm-tester` dispatches reviewers on **distinct but overlapping** briefs. The overlap is the
mechanism: two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two disagreeing is where
you learn something.

Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and **your measured gate numbers — then forbid them from
re-running the gates.** Their budget goes on what the gates cannot see.

Angles that have earned their place: correctness and regression · conventions, structure and tier
ownership · contract fidelity, if the PR ports, wraps or overrides something · failure modes and
security · token and styling strategy (bandaid tokens, missing semantic tokens, state
exhaustiveness).

**Design fidelity is yours, not an agent's.** Agents have no browser and no Figma access — ask
them to reason from code and they will, but they cannot see what renders. For any PR that changes
rendered output, run this checklist yourself at the PR's head:

| What to check | How |
|---|---|
| Dimensions and spacing match Figma frames | DevTools computed, vs. Figma inspect |
| Colours resolve to the correct semantic token | DevTools → Computed → colour value |
| Typography uses `textStyle=`, not raw `fontSize` | DevTools → font-size is a `var()` |
| All designed states render correctly (hover, focus, active, disabled) | Tab through + `:hov` in DevTools |
| Responsive behaviour matches the spec | Resize or toggle responsive mode |
| No visual regressions on adjacent components | Scroll the surrounding page |

If a state is not in the PR's recipe at all, no agent will flag it — only you will notice. The
visual checkpoint is the only gate on design fidelity.

Use **fresh contexts, not forks.** A fork inherits your assumptions about what "done" looks like,
which is exactly what you want tested.

### Scope

`zm-orchestrator` returns the scope verdict — does this PR deliver its ticket, neither under nor
over. Both directions carry equal weight.

### Verify the findings before they reach you

`zm-scorer`, briefed in **findings mode** — it is not scoring the PR, it is scoring the claims:

> For each finding: does it survive scrutiny? Reproduce it or say you could not. Return
> **CONFIRMED** (reproduced from source), **PLAUSIBLE** (consistent with what you read, decisive
> evidence missing — say exactly what would settle it), or **UNSUPPORTED** (the citation does not
> support the claim; say what is actually true). Where a finding's conclusion is broader than its
> search supports, downgrade it — that is the single most common failure mode. Any "X exists
> nowhere" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence.

Expect roughly a third to be wrong. You should not be adjudicating unverified claims.

**This applies to your own findings too, not just an agent's.** Anything you notice directly
while gathering ground truth (a comparison against a related PR, a claim sitting in a code
comment, an assumption about what a value implies) gets the same CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/UNSUPPORTED
discipline before it is presented as fact — a finding is not exempt from scrutiny just because no
agent produced it. Route it through the same questions: what is the search scope, does one
uncorroborated source actually settle this, and has a stated number been measured or only assumed.

### Classify every survivor

- **In-scope defect** — belongs to this PR. Only these can become comments.
- **Out-of-scope** — real, but not this PR's problem. Name the owning ticket or the person.
- **Nitpick** — cosmetic, brings no value. Recorded, never posted.

A true finding raised on the wrong PR is still noise.

---

## Phase 3 — adjudicate

### Present, in "ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead" register

1. **Gate table** — head versus base, with which checks actually executed
2. **Findings, ranked by what it costs to ignore** — not by severity label, by consequence.
   Each with `file:line`, CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE, and its classification
3. **The scope verdict**
4. **What nobody verified** — the honest section, and what stops a clean result reading as proof
5. **Your adjudications to make**, one at a time via AskUserQuestion

### The verdict is yours

**Approve or request changes is your call, and so is every disputed finding.** The agents produce
findings; you decide what they mean. Where two reviewers disagree, go to source yourself — do not
average them, and do not take the more confident one. Confidence and correctness are not correlated
in agent output.

Name one premise every reviewer agreed on, and make someone attack it.

### Then the comments

Draft general and inline comments for the in-scope defects only. Structure that has worked:

- Verdict up front
- The small cleanups separated from the one thing that genuinely needs the author's call
- A blocker framed as **a question about intent**, citing the project's own doc by section
- The two acceptable resolutions named
- Where an independent tool corroborated, say so

**Natural human language without sacrificing the technical accuracy.** No em-dashes. No Claude or
CodeRabbit attribution. No citation of any local-only doc — cite `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/*`
instead, which the author can actually open. No opening praise or thanks before the substance — a
review comment states findings, it does not warm up first. Watch for jargon-stacking too: a
sentence naming three technical concepts back to back reads like documentation, not like one
person explaining something to another — split it or say it plainer instead.

**Never reveal that a parallel or competing implementation of the same ticket exists**, even in
passing ("the other version of this feature," "the other build") — a review comment is visible to
the whole team, and disclosing a second, independent attempt at the same story is not this
reviewer's call to make. When a content rule like this applies, sweep every drafted comment for
it before presenting the batch, not just the one currently under discussion — a rule caught on
one comment and missed on a near-identical one is a leak, not a style nit.

**Nothing posts until you say so.** Show the full set, post the batch on your go.

---

## The loop

The author pushes changes. Re-review.

**Scoped by default:** which findings the new commits resolved, which they missed, and whether the
fixes introduced anything new. Settled items are not re-litigated.

**Full pass when the diff has genuinely moved** — a substantial new commit, or a change to the
approach rather than the details. **Say which one you ran.**

Repeat until approved. Confirm your own requested changes actually landed rather than taking
"done" on trust.

---

## Ownership and phrasing — every outward-facing surface

Every finding names **who resolves it**: the author, Tim, a designer, a BA, QA.

**Where the owner is senior or lateral, phrase it as a question — never a directive.** "Should this
route via X, or have I misread it?" not "change this to X." Ask confirmatorily.

Before posting, count the asks. A review that mentions one person eight times reads as hiding
behind their authority.

**Be scrupulously fair to the author.** Separate "broke a documented rule" from "hit a gap the
process never covered", and where the process failed them, say so. Flag explicitly any finding
where the fact is true but the characterisation is unfair — better to drop a finding than post an
unfair one.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never write code.** This skill reviews. If a fix is needed on your own branch, that is Build.
- **Never post a comment, a review, or a verdict without an explicit go.**
- **Never resolve a thread you did not open.**
- **Never report inherited debt as a new violation.** Baseline first.
- **Never flag out-of-scope findings onto the PR.** Record them for yourself.
- **Say what you could not verify.** A review that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable
  of finding anything.

The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- zm-implementer: Executes one step of a Zimmermann PWA Kit build plan. Use when a planned step needs to be implemented in code. Writes only the files the step names, and stops rather than expanding scope. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-orchestrator: Scope and spec-conformance checker for an in-flight Zimmermann build. Use after an implementation step to judge whether the work delivers exactly what the plan specified — neither less nor more. Reports a verdict; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-planner: Synthesises gathered evidence into an executable build plan for a Zimmermann PWA Kit story. Use after all sources have been gathered, when the findings need to become a sequenced plan with per-step pass criteria. Does not gather evidence itself and does not write code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch)

- zm-scorer: Scores an implemented and tested Zimmermann build step and decides PASS or return-to-implementer. Use after the Tester reports. Judges quality against six axes; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-tester: Tests an implemented Zimmermann build step across multiple angles and reports findings. Use after the Implementer reports a step done. Finds and reports problems; never fixes them. Dispatches its own sub-agents for parallel angles. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

name: SIT Gate

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - 'release/**'
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - 'release/**'

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: write
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  playwright-p0:
    name: Playwright P0 journeys
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        run: node_modules/.bin/playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - name: Run P0 suite
        run: node_modules/.bin/playwright test --project=p0 --reporter=html,github
        env:
          RETAIL_APP_HOME: ${{ vars.RETAIL_APP_HOME }}

      - name: Upload Playwright report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 30

      - name: Upload Pages artifact
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: playwright-report/

  deploy-playwright-report:
    name: Publish Playwright report to Pages
    needs: playwright-p0
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

  lighthouse-ci:
    name: Lighthouse CI
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    env:
      LHCI_SERVER_BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.LHCI_SERVER_BASE_URL }}
      LHCI_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.LHCI_TOKEN }}
      LHCI_TARGET_URL: ${{ secrets.LHCI_TARGET_URL_SIT }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      - name: Run Lighthouse CI
        run: node_modules/.bin/lhci autorun

      - name: Upload Lighthouse results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: lighthouse-results
          path: .lighthouseci/
          retention-days: 30

  contract-tests:
    name: MuleSoft contract tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      # TODO: Replace with real contract assertion once MuleSoft publishes OpenAPI specs.
      # Owner: Zimmermann integration team + Accenture delivery lead to align.
      - name: Run contract tests
        run: npm run test:contracts

  bundle-size:
    name: Bundle size check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      - name: Build and check bundle size
        run: npm run test:max-file-size

  sit-gate:
    name: SIT Gate
    needs: [playwright-p0, lighthouse-ci, contract-tests, bundle-size]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always()
    steps:
      - name: Check all SIT signals passed
        run: |
          if [ "${{ needs.playwright-p0.result }}" != "success" ] || \
             [ "${{ needs.lighthouse-ci.result }}" != "success" ] || \
             [ "${{ needs.contract-tests.result }}" != "success" ] || \
             [ "${{ needs.bundle-size.result }}" != "success" ]; then
            echo "SIT gate: one or more checks failed"
            echo "  playwright-p0:   ${{ needs.playwright-p0.result }}"
            echo "  lighthouse-ci:   ${{ needs.lighthouse-ci.result }}"
            echo "  contract-tests:  ${{ needs.contract-tests.result }}"
            echo "  bundle-size:     ${{ needs.bundle-size.result }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "SIT gate: all checks passed"

## What's Pending

New site ID `ZimmermannUSIntl` pending BM confirmation.

  - `qa.yml` (every PR to `develop`/`release/**`): `unit-tests` (Vitest) + `storybook-test` (Storybook `play` + `@storybook/addon-a11y`, `storybook test --ci`) run in parallel; `e2e-browserstack` on release PRs only. **`storybook-test` job is wired but pending `@storybook/addon-test` and `@storybook/addon-a11y` installation (feature/storybook-v10 upgrade task).**
  - `digital-sit.yml` (push/PR to `release/**`): four parallel jobs into `sit-gate` — `playwright-p0` (Chromium P0 suite), `bundle-size` (bundlewatch, main.js < 180 kB / vendor.js < 250 kB / main.css < 50 kB), `contract-tests` (placeholder; real MuleSoft OpenAPI assertion pending spec source), `lighthouse-ci` (Perf ≥ 80, A11y ≥ 90, Best Practices ≥ 90; requires LHCI server secrets)

Fixed by CodeRabbit-prompted review in PR #30 (separated `.click()` out of the `try/catch`) — but that fix was never actually exercised in CI until PR #35 re-enabled the job, confirmed via 4 consecutive clean CI passes. Along the way also: added an HTML reporter to `playwright.config.js` (every project except `p0` had been silently producing an empty `playwright-report/` — CI failures were undebuggable from artifacts alone); fixed a webpack-build-race (`wait-on` only confirms the port is open, not that the client bundle finished compiling — added a step polling `dev-server.log` for `webpack built client`); fixed the original missing-Commerce-API-env-vars bug (job now binds `environment: dev`, sources `COMMERCE_API_*` from `vars.*`, `scripts/switchEnv.mjs`'s `push <tier>` uploads a shared+tier merge so one environment binding is self-sufficient); switched the job gate from `always()` to `!cancelled()` so a superseded/cancelled run doesn't burn a 15-min runner slot.
- PR #30 (`feature/gh-qa-workflow`, merged) also: deleted the unfinished `SFCC-000_guest-checkout` placeholder (never had real Adyen payment interaction, self-described `EXAMPLE` in its own header) and its `testIgnore` mis-scoping (ran under `chromium`/`mobile-chrome` `retries:2` instead of the dedicated `p0` project's `retries:0`, costing ~12 of the ~14 min `e2e-localhost` runtime on every PR); added a homepage smoke test (new `homepage` E2E area + `SMOKE-` naming convention for Jira-less tests); fixed a `@typescript-eslint/no-var-requires` misconfiguration flagging `require()` in `e2e/`'s intentionally-CommonJS files; added `test-results/`/`playwright-report/` to `.gitignore`.
- **Proposed: tag-based environment promotion (GitFlow) — full spec on Confluence, implementation not yet started.** Full rationale, tag naming convention, worked commands, and open questions:
  [Proposed: Tag-Based Environment Promotion (GitFlow)](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/335216656/Proposed+Tag-Based+Environment+Promotion+GitFlow)
  (Confluence, v5, child of the Branching Guide page). Summary: only `Dev` should be continuously tied to `develop`; every other tier should deploy a specific, immutable git tag (`vX.Y.Z-rc.N` / `vX.Y.Z` / `vX.Y.Z-hotfix.N`, cut via `npm version`) instead of a branch ref, so Test/SIT/UAT/Stage can each run independent testing cycles instead of being forced onto the same moving branch. **Do not implement the AGENTS.md/governance pieces without squad-lead + Integration-lead sign-off — this is still a proposal.** Implementation checklist for a fresh session on a new branch (see the Confluence page for full detail on each item):
  - **Decided 2026-07-16** (see Confluence page's "Decisions made so far" table): release cadence is per-sprint; pre-launch versioning starts at `v0.1.0` (MAJOR locked at `0` until go-live, which becomes `v1.0.0`); `Test` gets its own automated CI gate (not manual-only); tag protection + the version-guard + Release-per-final-tag are all adopted immediately, not phased in.
  - **Tooling — safe to build now, doesn't touch governance docs:**
    1. `npm version` adoption — no code change needed, it's a built-in npm command; just start using it per the Confluence page's "How to deploy" section instead of raw `git tag`. First tag will be `v0.1.0-rc.0`.
    2. **Primary enforcement — one GitHub Ruleset covers both naming and immutability:** Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New tag ruleset, targeting `v*`, with a "tag name pattern" rule requiring `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-rc\.\d+|-hotfix\.\d+)?$` plus "restrict creation," "restrict updates," and "restrict deletion" all enabled. This genuinely hard-blocks a non-matching tag at push time *and* prevents force-push/delete on matching tags — all on GitHub.com, not Enterprise Server-only (corrected from an earlier draft of this note, which wrongly split this into a separate "tag protection rules" step and claimed pattern-blocking wasn't possible on GitHub.com). Keep a `push: tags: ['*']` validation workflow too, as defense-in-depth / for a clearer failure message than the raw ruleset rejection gives.
    3. A version-guard step added to each `deploy-*.yml` (test/sit/stg/uat/prod) — fetch the environment's current deployed tag via `gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/deployments?environment=<env>`, semver-compare against the tag being deployed (use the `semver` npm package, not hand-rolled bash comparison — pre-release identifiers must be dot-separated, e.g. `-rc.10` vs `-rc.2`, or numeric comparison breaks), fail on a downgrade. **`<env>` must be the actual GitHub Environment name, not the workflow-file suffix** — they diverge for `stg` (`deploy-stg.yml` targets the `staging` Environment, not `stg`; we hit this exact mismatch once already this session, commit `12bf91b`). Map each tier explicitly (`stg` → `staging`, everything else matches its filename) rather than deriving it from the filename. Fail closed if the environment name is wrong or the API call errors — a genuine first-ever deployment (no prior Deployment record at all) is fine to proceed, but an unresolvable environment/API error is not the same thing and must not be treated as "nothing to compare against, allow it."

    5. Wire `/generate-changelog`'s existing `gh release create` offer into the "cut the final tag" step — no new tooling, the skill already does this.

    7. `AGENTS.md`'s branch table / the Confluence Branching Guide itself, once the team has actually reviewed and approved the proposal — this repo's `AGENTS.md` requires both squad leads and the Integration lead to sign off on changes to itself, stronger than the usual verified-session Tier 1 exception.

# Release & Hotfix Branch Rules

**Read this file in full before taking any action when `git branch --show-current` matches `release/*` or `hotfix/*`.** These rules apply *in addition to* the Hard Rules in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md). On `feature/*` and `fix/*` branches they do not apply and this file can be ignored.

See the branch table in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) > Branch Rules for which branch merges where.

## Back-merge rules (GitFlow)

To prevent `develop` drifting from production:
- When a `release/*` branch is merged to `main` at go-live, it must also be merged back to `develop`.
- When a `hotfix/*` is merged to `main`, it must also be merged back to `develop`.
- When a `fix/release-*` is merged into its `release/*` parent and the release later ships, the forward-merge to `develop` happens as part of the release back-merge above — no separate action.

## Release Branch Behaviour

When on a `release/*` branch, the following rules apply in addition to all Hard Rules.

**Before writing any code, always:**
1. State a plan — which files will change, what will change in each, and why.
2. Assess blast radius — how many components, hooks, or pages consume each file being changed? Flag explicitly if any file has more than 3 consumers or is Tier 2 or above.
3. Wait for explicit developer confirmation before making any edit, including trivial ones.

**Allowed on release branches:**
- Read-only skills: `/generate-changelog`, `/pr-checklist`, `/code-quality`
- Trivial non-code changes (copy corrections, version bumps, feature flag toggles) — plan + confirm required
- Code logic fixes — only on a `fix/release-{version}_{description}` sub-branch, never directly on the release branch

**Not allowed on release branches:**
- New features or scope additions not in the release
- Refactoring
- Dependency changes
- Tier 1 or Tier 2 file changes without the same owner approval required on feature branches

**How to make a code fix on a release branch:**

The fix PR targets the release branch. Once the release ships, the fix flows into `develop` via the release back-merge — do not open a separate PR from `fix/release-*` to `develop`.

```bash
# Branch from the release branch — not from develop
git checkout release/v0.1.0
git checkout -b fix/release-v0.1.0-payment-error-description

# Make the fix, open a PR targeting the release branch
gh pr create --base release/v0.1.0 --title "fix(checkout): SFCC-999 payment error on release"
```
The SIT gate will run against the PR before it can merge (when CI lands). See [architecture.md > Environments](architecture.md) for the full environment topology (Local · Dev · Test · SIT · UAT · Stage · Prod).

      },

- Baseline (pre-PR, 2026-08-05 run on release/v0.1.0): `playwright-p0` hard-failed "No tests found"; `lighthouse-ci` failed with `CHROME_INTERSTITIAL_ERROR` hitting `http://localhost:3000` (because `LHCI_TARGET_URL_SIT` secret was unset, so `LHCI_TARGET_URL` env resolved empty and the `|| 'http://localhost:3000'` fallback kicked in against nothing listening). Confirmed via actual job logs — Tim's PR description accurately diagnoses this.
- On this PR's own head run: `playwright-p0` now SUCCEEDS via soft-pass, and the `::warning title=No P0 coverage::...` annotation fired exactly as designed (confirmed in the actual job log). This part works correctly, verified.
- `lighthouse-ci` on this PR's head run no longer hits CHROME_INTERSTITIAL_ERROR — it successfully reaches the real SIT MRT URL (confirmed: "Uploading median LHR of ***...success!" — it collected 3 real runs and uploaded to the LHCI server). So the URL/header fix works mechanically. BUT the job still fails (exit 1) because of 12 real `error`-level assertion failures against actual (bad) site performance: `categories.performance` found 0.41 vs expected ≥0.8, `categories.best-practices` found 0.83 vs expected ≥0.9, plus `csp-xss`, `errors-in-console`, `inspector-issues`, `installable-manifest`, `maskable-icon`, `service-worker`, `splash-screen`, `unused-javascript`, `uses-rel-preconnect`, `valid-source-maps` all at 0/failing (all part of the pre-existing, untouched `lighthouse:recommended` preset — Tim's diff did not change `assert.preset` or the assertions block at all). `categories.accessibility` passed. This is a genuine, pre-existing site-quality gap on whatever `develop` build Tim manually deployed to SIT (via `npm run push:sit`, mentioned in the PR body as a manual action, not part of the diff) — NOT something introduced by or fixable within this 2-file diff. I'm treating this as correctly out of scope for this PR — do not report it as a defect in the diff itself. I already plan to flag it separately as a discovery, not as an in-scope finding.
- "Publish Playwright report to Pages" job (a separate job in the same workflow, NOT touched by this diff, NOT part of the `sit-gate` job's `needs:` list) fails identically on both the baseline run and this PR's run — empty `steps` array both times, meaning it fails during job setup (consistent with a GitHub Pages/environment config issue). Confirmed pre-existing baseline debt via direct comparison of both runs' job lists — not in scope, don't re-flag it as new.
- Both changed files (`lighthouserc.js`, `.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml`) are Tier 1 per `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md` and correctly routed to `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` in `CODEOWNERS` (lines for `lighthouserc.js` and `.github/workflows/`). The repo's `tier1-guard` check fired correctly and listed both files. This part of the process is working correctly — don't re-verify unless you spot something I'd have missed (e.g. a glob gap in CODEOWNERS that doesn't actually match one of these two exact paths — worth a quick double check).
- `node -c lighthouserc.js` passes (valid JS syntax) at head.

## What I need from you

**(a) Correctness/regression:**
1. Read `playwright.config.*` (read-only — it's Tier 1 test config, don't propose editing it) and confirm the `p0` project's test-matching pattern actually aligns with the `find e2e/tests/zimm -name '*.p0.spec.*'` glob this PR's new warning step uses. I want to know if the glob is a faithful proxy for "playwright will actually match zero p0 tests," or if it could drift out of sync (e.g., if the p0 project's `testMatch` is scoped differently than a flat `*.p0.spec.*` search under `e2e/tests/zimm`). Check `.claude/rules/testing.md`'s documented naming convention too (`SFCC-NNN_description.p0.spec.ts`) for corroboration.
2. Is `--pass-with-no-tests` a real, documented Playwright Test CLI flag? Confirm via `node_modules/@playwright/test` or `node_modules/playwright/` docs/source if present, or via package.json's playwright version and known CLI flags for that version.
3. Any bug in the bash conditional (`if ! find ... | grep -q .; then ... fi`) — edge cases, quoting, exit-code handling.
4. Does `extraHeaders: ... : undefined` behave correctly when `LHCI_SFDC_ACCESS_CONTROL` is unset (i.e., does passing `extraHeaders: undefined` to lighthouse-ci's `collect.settings` behave the same as omitting the key entirely, or could it throw / behave unexpectedly)? Check `node_modules/@lhci/cli` or `node_modules/lighthouse` if helpful, or reason from how the config is consumed.
5. Check other workflows (`deploy-test.yml`, `deploy-sit.yml` if it exists, any other `.github/workflows/*.yml` referencing `LHCI_TARGET_URL` or Lighthouse) for naming consistency — does this PR's approach (secret `LHCI_TARGET_URL_SIT` mapped to generic env var `LHCI_TARGET_URL`) match a pattern used elsewhere, or could it collide/confuse across tiers?

**(b) Security/failure-modes:**
1. Could the real value of `LHCI_SFDC_ACCESS_CONTROL` leak into any artifact with broader read access than "GitHub Actions secrets + the SIT environment itself"? Specifically: does a standard `lhci autorun` LHR JSON (what gets written to `.lighthouseci/` and/or uploaded to an LHCI server) ever include raw request headers sent during the Lighthouse run? I believe standard LHR JSON's `audits['network-requests']` does NOT include request headers (only url/timing/size/status fields) — verify this against the actual installed `lighthouse`/`@lhci/cli` package in `node_modules` if you can find schema/source evidence, and tell me if my belief is right, wrong, or unconfirmable from what's available in this repo. Note GitHub's own log redaction already confirmed masking the literal secret value in log text (`LHCI_SFDC_ACCESS_CONTROL: ***`), so the concern is specifically about the LHR JSON artifact/LHCI-server-stored content, not the Action log.
2. Any other secret-handling issue in the diff (e.g., a secret echoed in a way that wouldn't be auto-masked, a secret passed on a command line where it'd show in `ps`, etc.)?
3. Does the new header get sent anywhere it shouldn't (e.g., to the `http://localhost:3000` fallback path when running against a non-SIT target)? Confirm the ternary correctly scopes it to only when `LHCI_SFDC_ACCESS_CONTROL` is actually set.

Report findings in the standard format (file:line, summary, failure scenario, category). Be precise about CONFIRMED vs something you couldn't fully verify — say what would settle it if you can't. Keep the report tight; this is a small diff, I don't need padding.

# Autonomous loop check

You're being invoked on a timer while the user is away or occupied. The point is to keep work moving forward without the user driving every step - finishing things they started, maintaining PRs they're building, catching problems before they come back to find them. You're a steward, not an initiator. The user set you loose on their work, and the value you provide comes from reliably advancing things they've already set in motion, not from finding new things to do.

The key tension to navigate: the user trusts you enough to run autonomously, but that trust is easily lost. Acting on what the conversation already established is safe and valuable. Inventing new work or making irreversible changes without clear authorization erodes trust fast. When you're unsure whether something falls into "continuing established work" or "inventing new work," lean toward the former only when the transcript provides clear evidence the user wanted it done. If you find yourself reaching for justifications about why a push is probably fine, that's a signal to wait.

## What to act on

The current conversation is your highest-signal source - re-read the transcript above, since everything there is something the user was actively engaged with. The strongest signal is an in-progress PR you've been building together: review comments to address and resolve, failing CI checks to diagnose (and re-enqueue if they're flakes), merge conflicts to fix. The goal is to get the PR into a state where it's ready to merge pending only human review - the user shouldn't come back to find a PR blocked on things you could have handled. After that, look for unfinished implementation where the last exchange left something half-done, and explicit "I'll also..." or "next I'll..." commitments the conversation made and didn't honor. Weaker but still real: dangling questions you could now answer, verification steps that were skipped, edge cases that were mentioned but not handled, and natural continuations that don't require new decisions.

If you find anything in this category, act on it - actually do the work, don't describe what could be done. Run the tests, don't say "you could run the tests." The whole point of autonomous operation is that work gets done while the user is away.

When the conversation transcript has nothing left, the current branch's pull/merge request on the user's SCM is the next-best place to look. This is maintenance work - valuable, but lower priority than continuing the user's active work. Find the PR/MR for the current branch via the SCM's CLI, then check three things: CI status, unresolved review threads, and whether the branch has fallen behind the base. For failing CI, pull the failing job's logs and diagnose before acting - flaky-shaped failures (timeout, runner died, transient network) can be re-enqueued; real failures need a reproduction and a minimal fix. For unresolved review threads, fetch the comment, address the feedback, push, and resolve the thread via, for example, the GitHub GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation (or the equivalent for whichever SCM the project uses). Before pushing anything, check whether someone else has pushed to the branch while you were working - if so, rebase (don't merge) to keep history clean.

When CI is green, threads are clear, and there's idle time, sweeping the branch for issues is a good use of that time - bug-hunt or simplification passes catch problems before reviewers do, saving everyone a round-trip.

If everything is genuinely quiet - no conversation work, no PR maintenance - say so in one sentence and stop. No summary of what you checked, no list of what you might do later. The user will see your message in the transcript when they come back; three consecutive "nothing to do" results means you should scale back to a quick CI check and stop, not narrate.

## Repeated invocations

If you see earlier autonomous checks in this conversation, adjust your scope accordingly. If a previous check left a question the user hasn't answered, the cost of acting depends on reversibility: for reversible actions (local edits, running tests), make your best call and proceed; for irreversible ones (pushing, deleting, sending), keep waiting - the cost of acting wrongly on something irreversible is much higher than the cost of waiting one more cycle. If three or more consecutive checks have found nothing actionable, things are quiet - do one quick CI/threads check and stop in a single line. Repeated "nothing to do" messages clutter the transcript and waste the user's attention when they come back to review.

Read and analyze freely - understanding the state of things has no blast radius. Make edits and run tests when you're confident they continue established work. Commit and push only when you're clearly continuing something the user authorized, or when the work pattern makes the intent obvious - like fixing CI on a PR you've been building together.

All three findings — including the secret-leakage issue — came back **CONFIRMED**, with the scorer independently reproducing the leak live (not just re-reading the tester's source trace) and independently reproducing the P0 scope-mismatch bug too. Here's the full picture.

## Gate table

| Check | Baseline (2026-08-05, pre-PR) | This PR's head run | Ran? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Playwright P0 journeys | FAILURE ("No tests found") | **SUCCESS** (soft-pass + warning fired correctly) | Yes |
| Lighthouse CI | FAILURE (`CHROME_INTERSTITIAL_ERROR`, hit unserved `localhost:3000`) | **FAILURE** — different cause: real scores (Perf 0.41 < 0.8, Best Practices 0.83 < 0.9, +10 more) against real SIT content | Yes |
| MuleSoft contract tests | SUCCESS | SUCCESS | Yes |
| Bundle size check | SUCCESS | SUCCESS | Yes |
| Publish Playwright report to Pages | FAILURE (fails at job-setup, before any step) | FAILURE (identical) | Pre-existing baseline debt, not this PR's issue |
| SIT Gate (summary) | FAILURE | FAILURE (blocked by lighthouse-ci) | Yes |
| Tier 1 — Frozen Files Check | — | SUCCESS (correctly flagged both files as Tier 1) | Yes |
| CodeRabbit | — | **Skipped entirely** — auto-review is disabled for non-default-branch targets, so there's no automated review on this PR at all | Ran, produced nothing |
| Unit/Storybook/E2E-localhost/BrowserStack | — | Skipped | Expected — no e2e-relevant paths in a 2-file CI-config diff |

`mergeStateStatus: BLOCKED`, `reviewDecision: REVIEW_REQUIRED` — pending review from `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` (Tim can't self-approve his own Tier-1 files; I'm confirmed on that team, `hanl` is the other option).

## Findings, ranked by cost of ignoring

**1. Blocking — secret leak, confirmed by live reproduction.** `lighthouserc.js`'s new `extraHeaders` block forwards `LHCI_SFDC_ACCESS_CONTROL`'s real value into Lighthouse's settings. That settings object isn't stripped anywhere in the `@lhci/cli` → `lighthouse` pipeline before being embedded verbatim in `configSettings` on the final report — confirmed by actually running this exact code path locally with a fake secret and watching it land in plaintext in both the generated LHR JSON *and* the HTML report. `digital-sit.yml`'s existing "Upload Lighthouse results" step (untouched by this PR, but newly dangerous because of it) uploads that whole directory as a 30-day GitHub Actions artifact, and the same report is pushed to the external LHCI server via the pre-existing `LHCI_SERVER_BASE_URL` upload — confirmed that upload actually fired on this PR's own real CI run. Net effect: the credential that gates access to SIT ends up persisted somewhere broader than "people who can read the GitHub secret." Secondary, coupled issue: `.gitignore` doesn't exclude `.lighthouseci/` either, so a local `lhci autorun` with this var set risks committing the secret straight into git history.

**2. Should-fix, confirmed by reproduction.** The new "Warn if no P0 specs exist yet" step checks `find e2e/tests/zimm -name '*.p0.spec.*'`, but `playwright.config.js`'s `p0` project has no `testDir` override (unlike `a11y-*`, which does scope its own), so it actually collects `*.p0.spec.{js,ts}` anywhere under `e2e/`. A real P0 spec placed outside `e2e/tests/zimm/` would run for real while this check still claims zero coverage — the dangerous direction, since it could make a working gate look fake. Dormant today (no specs exist anywhere yet), one-line fix.

**3. Not a defect — a question of intent, worth putting to Tim directly.** All three reviewers converged on treating the real Lighthouse failure (Perf/Best-Practices/PWA-installability/CSP gaps) as correctly out of scope for a CI-recovery PR — nothing in this diff could move those numbers. I want to press on that consensus rather than just accept it: Tim already invented a "soft-pass + loud warning" pattern for exactly this shape of problem on the P0 side (real gap, early-stage app, permanently-blocking gate) — he didn't apply the same pattern to Lighthouse. That's either a deliberate call (perf debt is more dangerous to let slide than test debt, so it should stay a hard blocker) or an inconsistency worth naming. Compounding this: `deploy-sit.yml` only auto-redeploys SIT when the *entire* SIT Gate passes — so with Lighthouse now failing for real, SIT won't refresh automatically again until performance work lands. Tim's manual bootstrap may end up being the last fresh SIT content for a while, not a one-off unblock.

## What nobody verified

- Whether these four LHCI secrets are plain repo-level Actions secrets or environment-scoped — not visible from source, doesn't change the leak finding either way.
- Exactly why this PR's own real run showed "no files found" for the local `.lighthouseci/` artifact (the reproduction sandbox reliably produced files under the same real packages) — a timing/working-directory quirk most likely, but not fully pinned down. Doesn't weaken the finding: the LHCI-server upload path independently fired for real on this exact run regardless.
- Whether `.env.sample` registration is actually expected for CI-runner-only secrets like this — genuinely ambiguous from AGENTS.md's own wording, and the same gap already exists on this secret's three siblings, so I'm not raising it as a PR-specific issue.

Two adjudications I'd like your steer on before I draft anything:
